content: Infectious mononucleosis, also referred to as glandular fever or the kissing disease, is a benign lymphoproliferative disorder caused by the Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). EBV is a herpesvirus that is widespread across all human populations and cultures. Epidemiological studies indicate that over 95% of adults globally have been infected with EBV at some point in their lives. Symptomatic cases of infectious mononucleosis are most commonly observed in individuals aged 15 to 24 years. The virus is primarily transmitted through close contact with an individual shedding EBV, exposure to infected saliva, or, less frequently, through sexual contact, blood transfusions, or sharing utensils. However, the actual rate of transmission is relatively low, occurring in less than 10% of exposures. Due to the high prevalence of EBV seropositivity in the population, specific precautions to prevent transmission are generally not necessary. Infectious mononucleosis is a self-limiting condition, with symptoms typically resolving within two to three weeks. However, in some cases, symptoms may persist for several weeks or even months. Common symptoms include fever, lymphadenopathy, pharyngitis, hepatosplenomegaly, and fatigue. Standard management often involves symptomatic relief and rest. Steroids have been employed for their anti-inflammatory properties, but there are no universally accepted guidelines for their use in this condition. The objective of the review was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of steroid therapy compared to placebo, standard care, or other pharmacological interventions for symptom management in infectious mononucleosis. For the 2015 update, a comprehensive search was conducted in databases such as the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, and EMBASE, covering studies up to August 2015. Additionally, trial registries were reviewed, but no new relevant completed or ongoing trials were identified. The search strategy was tailored to identify randomized controlled trials (RCTs) specifically. The inclusion criteria focused on RCTs that compared the effectiveness of steroids with placebo, usual care, or other interventions for symptom control in individuals with confirmed infectious mononucleosis. Standard Cochrane methodological procedures were employed for data collection and analysis. The 2015 update did not identify any new RCTs for inclusion. The previous version of the review included seven trials with a total of 362 participants. Four trials compared steroids to placebo for short-term symptom control, one trial compared steroids to aspirin, and two trials investigated the combination of steroids with an antiviral agent. Due to heterogeneity among the trials, a pooled analysis was not feasible. Methodological limitations were noted, as three trials did not adequately describe the randomization process, and four trials provided sufficient details on allocation concealment. While all trials were double-blinded, four did not specify the individuals who were blinded. Additionally, loss to follow-up was under-reported in four trials, raising concerns about potential attrition bias. The risk of selective reporting was unclear across the included trials. In terms of outcomes, no significant benefit of steroid therapy was observed in 8 out of 10 assessments of health improvement. Two trials demonstrated a short-term benefit of steroids over placebo in reducing sore throat at 12 hours. Specifically, an eight-day course of steroids showed an odds ratio (OR) of 21.00 (95% confidence interval [CI] 1.94 to 227.20), and a single dose showed an OR of 4.20 (95% CI 1.08 to 16.32). However, this benefit was not sustained over time. When combined with an antiviral drug, steroids were associated with reduced pharyngeal discomfort between days two and four (OR 0.31, 95% CI 0.09 to 1.08) compared to placebo. The effects of steroids on other common symptoms were less conclusive. Two trials specifically assessed the safety of steroid therapy and reported no major adverse effects. However, two other trials documented adverse events, including respiratory distress and acute onset of diabetes. The causal relationship between these events and steroid use was not definitively established. In conclusion, there is insufficient evidence to support the efficacy of steroids for symptom control in infectious mononucleosis. Furthermore, there is a lack of robust research on the potential side effects and long-term complications associated with steroid use in this context.
